title: Why the Cloud Won
objective: After this level you can explain why companies rent computing from cloud providers instead of running their own servers, and what they give up.
summary: Cloud computing swaps buying servers for elastic, metered capacity that follows demand, cheaper through economies of scale; the price is control, while responsibility stays with you.

cards.headline: Own the computers, or rent them?
cards.body: Owning means buying machines up front, before you know exactly how busy you'll be. Renting from a cloud provider turns that big purchase into running costs that follow what you actually use. So why did renting win so many companies over, and what do they trade away?

cards.headline: Pay for what you use
cards.body: NIST, the US standards agency, lists what makes a service a cloud. Two features matter most for the bill. Rapid elasticity: capacity can be added and released quickly, sometimes automatically, as demand rises and falls, so to the customer it can seem unlimited. Measured service: storage, processing and bandwidth are metered, like electricity. Busy week? Rent more. Quiet night? Hand it back.

cards.headline: Why sharing is cheaper
cards.body: A cloud provider pools its machines to serve many customers, gaining economies of scale that a single company can't reach alone. For the customer, the cloud swaps a large capital investment in computers for operating costs that track real use, and it can lower the up-front cost of launching something new. No room full of idle servers required.

cards.headline: What you give up
cards.body: Control. Moving to a public cloud hands control of data and systems to the provider, and NIST warns that the customer then depends on the provider's cooperation for jobs like monitoring and responding to incidents. Yet the customer stays accountable for the security and privacy of what it moved. You can rent the computers. You can't rent out the responsibility.

cards.headline: The cloud: weighed
learned: The cloud turns buying servers into metered running costs
Rapid elasticity: add and release capacity as demand shifts
Pooling many customers brings economies of scale
The provider gains control; you keep the responsibility

questions.prompt: In NIST's definition of cloud computing, what does "rapid elasticity" mean?

options.label: Capacity can be added and released quickly as demand changes
Servers are built to bend without breaking
options.rationale: It's about capacity, not physical toughness.

options.label: Prices change every hour with the weather
options.rationale: Elasticity is about scaling capacity up and down.

options.label: Data is stretched across as many drives as possible
options.rationale: It describes adding and releasing capacity.

questions.explanation: Rapid elasticity means capacity can be provisioned and released quickly, sometimes automatically, as demand rises and falls.

questions.prompt: Why can a cloud provider offer computing more cheaply than one company running its own servers?

options.label: Its computers run without needing any electricity
options.rationale: Cloud machines use plenty of power.

options.label: It never has to replace its hardware
It avoids paying for any network connections
It pools machines for many customers: economies of scale

questions.explanation: Pooling resources across many customers gives providers economies of scale that one company alone can't reach.

questions.prompt: A shop rents extra cloud capacity for a big sale, then hands it back. What has it given up by not owning the machines?

options.label: Its responsibility for its customers' data
options.rationale: NIST says the customer stays accountable for security and privacy.

options.label: Direct control, while staying accountable for security
The ability to pay only for what it used
options.rationale: Metered service is exactly what it gained.

options.label: Any way to add capacity quickly next time
options.rationale: Rapid elasticity lets it scale again whenever needed.

questions.explanation: Renting brings elastic, metered capacity, but control passes to the provider while accountability stays with the customer.
